title: Mitsui Chemicals and DBJ Buy Chip Materials Maker JSR for $11.6B, Huawei Unveils a Fully Domestic PC, and Nvidia's Board Opens a Formal Probe After CEO Admits Affair
subhead: A Japanese state-backed consortium led by Mitsui Chemicals and the Development Bank of Japan filed to acquire semiconductor materials leader JSR for $11.6 billion, while Huawei announced a PC built with 100 percent Chinese components and Chinese researchers demonstrated a 94 percent accurate brain-computer interface. In Silicon Valley, Nvidia's board launched an independent investigation after CEO Jensen Huang admitted to an extramarital affair with an executive suspected of ties to Chinese intelligence, and OpenAI hired former Army Secretary Dan Driscoll to lead cybersecurity.

sections.heading: Mitsui Chemicals and DBJ File $11.6B Buyout of JSR as Huawei Claims 100% Chinese PC
sections.body:
Mitsui Chemicals and the state-backed Development Bank of Japan (DBJ) will acquire Japanese semiconductor materials manufacturer JSR Corp. for $11.6 billion, according to a regulatory filing reported by CNA on Monday, consolidating Tokyo's control over global photoresists and advanced chipmaking chemicals. Elsewhere in East Asia, South Korea's government announced Monday that ongoing governance and security investigations at Nvidia will not affect South Korea's contracted supplies of Nvidia GPUs (CNA).

In China, Huawei announced that it has produced a personal computer built with 100 percent Chinese-made components, eliminating reliance on US processors and operating systems (The Register). Separately, Chinese researchers unveiled a non-invasive electrode for brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) that achieved over 94 percent accuracy in visual mind-typing tests during day-long use, while in Southeast Asia, Apple completed its largest-ever educational Mac deployment in the Philippines and analysts warned that government adoption of AI across Southeast Asia is shrinking civil-service hiring ladders for the middle class (SCMP, The Register).
sections.whyItMatters: Japan's $11.6 billion consolidation of photoresist giant JSR and Huawei's fully domestic PC illustrate how Asian tech powers are locking down opposite ends of the semiconductor stack — upstream chemical monopolies in Tokyo and de-Americanized hardware in Shenzhen.

sections.heading: Nvidia Board Opens Independent Probe as Huang Admits Affair; Trump Backs CEO
sections.body:
Nvidia's board of directors announced on Sunday that it has opened a formal independent investigation into founder and chief executive Jensen Huang after Huang admitted in a message to employees that he had been unfaithful to his wife in an affair with a Chinese businesswoman suspected by US intelligence of passing information to Beijing (New York Times, Bloomberg, Financial Times, Wall Street Journal, BBC). According to the New York Times, Secretary of State Marco Rubio played a direct role this past spring in drafting a secret memo warning senior officials about Huang's entanglement with the executive, who reportedly purchased GPUs in bulk (New York Times, The Register).

Huang apologized to his family, employees, and customers and pledged full cooperation with the board's independent committee, while Nvidia stated there is currently no evidence that classified data or national security assets were compromised (AP News, CBS News, Dünya). On Sunday night, President Donald Trump publicly defended Huang despite the investigation, and separately told Reuters that artificial intelligence risks can be managed while signaling openness to regulatory guardrails (Bloomberg, Axios, Reuters).
sections.whyItMatters: A formal board investigation into the CEO of the world's most valuable chipmaker — triggered by a State Department counterintelligence memo — turns executive personal security into a boardroom governance and export-control issue.

sections.heading: OpenAI Hires Ex-Army Secretary Dan Driscoll for Cyber as Global Infrastructure Hacks Mount
sections.body:
OpenAI has hired former US Army Secretary Dan Driscoll to a senior cybersecurity role, according to the Wall Street Journal, bolstering its national-security leadership days after closing its $11 billion funding round. In the venture capital market, former Secret Service agent and ex-Home Depot CISO Stephen Ward is raising a second cybersecurity fund of roughly $250 million at Brightmind Partners, while enterprise chief information security officers told the Wall Street Journal that North Korea's $6.3 billion Binance heist — after which Binance resumed withdrawals on Sunday — reflects the escalating scale of state-backed threats facing corporate networks (TechCrunch, Wall Street Journal).

Civilian infrastructure and state agencies faced a wave of attacks over the weekend. Authorities in the United States and internationally are investigating a series of cyberattacks and bomb threats targeting supermarkets and water control systems, while Japan declared an information security emergency (CBS News, The Register). In Eastern Europe, hacker collectives Silent Crown and Belarus Cyber Partisans breached Russia's state statistics agency Rosstat, and cybersecurity researchers warned in The Register that autonomous AI agents readily divulge confidential secrets when prompted to collaborate with other agents (The Independent, The Register).
sections.whyItMatters: OpenAI's recruitment of a former Army Secretary alongside attacks on water utilities and state statistical agencies underscores the convergence of frontier AI labs with national cyber defense.

sections.heading: ITU Confronts 278 Internet Governance Proposals as Türk Telekom Wires COP31 With 400 Gbps
sections.body:
Global internet governance faces its quadrennial stress test at the upcoming International Telecommunication Union (ITU) meeting, where delegates will debate 278 proposals that Western network operators fear could shift technical standard-setting power toward national governments (The Register). Meanwhile, a team of researchers in Germany solved the mystery behind coordinated power-frequency disturbances that have repeatedly haunted electrical grids worldwide, while physicists used electrical noise measurements to verify electron pairing in superconductors (TechCrunch, Ars Technica).

In corporate governance and mobility, Sequoia Capital partners were reportedly blindsided when former senior steward Roelof Botha joined the board of SpaceX, enterprise CIOs told the Wall Street Journal they are tightening scrutiny on measurable AI returns, and Apple Chairman Tim Cook arrived in Istanbul for a visit (TechCrunch, Wall Street Journal, Bloomberg HT). In Antalya, Türk Telekom deployed 1.3 million meters of fiber-optic cable, 16 new base stations, 1,800 Wi-Fi access points, and 400 Gbps connectivity staffed by 1,500 engineers to power the 1.1-million-square-meter COP31 summit venue (Dünya, Anadolu Agency, Yeni Şafak).
sections.whyItMatters: The 278 proposals on the table at the ITU meeting highlight an intensifying diplomatic push by state-centric telecom blocs to bring AI, satellite, and core internet routing standards under intergovernmental control.

bottomLine: Semiconductor supply chains and executive counterintelligence led Monday's technology agenda. In Tokyo, Mitsui Chemicals and the Development Bank of Japan filed an $11.6 billion buyout of chip-materials leader JSR just as Huawei unveiled a 100 percent Chinese-built PC and South Korea moved to reassure markets that its contracted Nvidia GPU deliveries remain intact. That reassurance followed Sunday's announcement by Nvidia's board of an independent investigation into CEO Jensen Huang after he admitted to an affair with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset — a case Secretary of State Marco Rubio flagged in a secret spring memo, though President Trump publicly backed Huang on Sunday night. Meanwhile, OpenAI hired former Army Secretary Dan Driscoll for cybersecurity as hackers targeted water utilities and Russia's Rosstat agency.
